headline: rails/rails
abstract: Ruby on Railshttps://rubyonrails.orgWelcome to Rails What's Rails? Rails is a web application framework that includes everything needed to create database-backed web applications according to the Model-View-Controller (MVC) pattern. Understanding the MVC pattern is key to understanding Rails. MVC divides your application into three layers: Model, View, and Controller, each with a specific responsibility. Model layer The Model layer represents the domain model (such as Account, Product, Person, Post, etc.) and encapsulates the business logic specific to your application. In Rails, database-backed model classes are derived from ActiveRecord::Base. Active Record allows you to present the data from database rows as objects and embellish these data objects with business logic methods. Although most Rails models are backed by a database, models can also be ordinary Ruby classes, or Ruby classes that implement a set of interfaces as provided by the Active Model module. View layer The View layer is composed of "templates" that are responsible for providing appropriate representations of your application's resources. Templates can come in a variety of formats, but most view templates are HTML with embedded Ruby code (ERB files). Views are typically rendered to generate a controller response or to generate the body of an email. In Rails,...

headline: The interesting thing about AI agents is that as a theoretical matter, their inference can kind of run anywhere. AI is one of the few areas of technology that isn’t *as* sensitive to latency back to the user. Long running agents are now going to be the norm, which means it’s ok to send off work to an AI factory somewhere and that work can essentially be largely done within that remote data center and a final result spit back to the user. The data can pass into these systems in an encrypted manner, be combed through by agents, and then disregarded right after. And because the economic value of the task is so high relative to the latency sensitivity (eg getting back $500 in value from an automated task, but it takes an extra second to return), you don’t have to have the inference to be particularly close to the user. Also, because inference is a temporary process with no sensitive data needing to be stored long term where the inference is happening, you can effectively treat AI factories as ephemeral systems, changing some of the data residency dynamics slightly. Combined, this means you have more flexibility in where you can begin to deploy AI data centers. This is both a huge economic opportunity for the states or countries (or space) that want to take advantage of this fact. And it’s a loss to the states or countries that decide to forgo the opportunity.
